extracted.intended_audience: students and readers of logic and philosophy; logicians and philosophers
extracted.subtask_description: A textbook-style analysis and taxonomy of names and propositions: their forms, varieties, import, and how to interpret and classify different kinds of propositions (affirmative/negative, simple/compound, hypothetical/categorical, universal/particular/singular, etc.).

rubrics_metrics.name: Copula as sign of predication (not existence)
rubrics_metrics.description: The copula (e.g., 'is', 'is not') functions as the sign that a predication is being made; its use as a copula does not necessarily imply existence.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Distinguish the copula's grammatical function from existential claims. Example: 'Socrates is just' does not by virtue of the copula alone imply 'Socrates is' (exists); contrast with 'A centaur is a fiction of the poets' which shows copula can occur without implying existence. Beware confounding the copula's role with metaphysical claims about Being — ambiguity of 'to be' has caused much metaphysical error. Historical note: James Mill emphasized this ambiguity; Hobbes and others treated negatives differently (see below).

rubrics_metrics.name: Affirmative vs Negative propositions
rubrics_metrics.description: Propositions divide into affirmative (predicate affirmed of subject) and negative (predicate denied of subject).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Negative copula commonly expressed by 'is not'. Alternative analysis (Hobbes) treats 'is' as sole copula and attaches negation to the predicate (treating 'not-dead' as the predicate), but this is criticized as verbal simplification that obscures the real distinction between asserting a fact and asserting its non-existence. Practical implication: do not collapse affirmation and denial into mere lexical tricks; the distinction corresponds to a real difference in fact and non-fact.

rubrics_metrics.name: Temporal modality attaches to the copula
rubrics_metrics.description: Tense or time (past/present/future) properly attaches to the copula (the sign of predication), not to the predicate itself.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Interpret 'The sun did rise / is rising / will rise' as the time qualification of the predication rather than an intrinsic difference in the predicate 'rise'. Treat tense as affecting the applicability of the predicate to the subject. For modal qualifiers like 'may' or 'perhaps', note these often express our mental state (epistemic attitude) rather than a property of the fact itself (see modal/epistemic distinction below).

rubrics_metrics.name: Simple (single) vs Compound (complex) propositions
rubrics_metrics.description: Simple proposition: one subject and one predicate. Compound/complex proposition: more than one subject or predicate (or both).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Recognize many 'complex' propositions joined by conjunctions ('and','but') are in effect multiple distinct propositions rather than a single assertion; conjunctions/punctuation often abbreviate separate propositions. Distinguish true compounds that convey a single assertion (e.g., conditionals, disjunctions) from mere aggregates of propositions. Example of blended expressions: 'Peter and James preached at Jerusalem and in Galilee' encodes multiple simple propositions for brevity.

rubrics_metrics.name: Hypothetical/Conditional vs Categorical propositions
rubrics_metrics.description: Hypothetical (conditional) propositions assert that one proposition is a legitimate inference from another; categorical propositions assert without condition.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Treat the subject and predicate of a conditional as names of propositions (the subject being a whole proposition, the predicate an assertion about inference). Example: 'If the Koran comes from God, Mohammed is the prophet of God' asserts inferability, not the truth of either component proposition. Disjunctive propositions ('either...or') can be rephrased as conditionals; understand how particles abbreviate inferential relations.

rubrics_metrics.name: Disjunctive propositions resolvable into conditionals
rubrics_metrics.description: 'Either A is B or C is D' is equivalent to a set of conditionals: 'If A is not B, C is D' and 'If C is not D, A is B'.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use this equivalence to analyze the logical form and inferential content of disjunctions. Recognize the relation between disjunction and conditional forms when evaluating logical import.

rubrics_metrics.name: Classification by generality: Universal, Particular, Indefinite, Singular
rubrics_metrics.description: Propositions classified according to the degree of generality of the subject: Universal (predicate of all members), Particular (predicate of some unspecified members), Indefinite (form unclear between universal/particular), Singular (subject is an individual).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: 'All men are mortal' (Universal); 'Some men are mortal' (Particular); 'Man is mortal' often read as Universal though grammatically indefinite; 'Julius Caesar is mortal' (Singular). Be cautious with 'indefinite' — Whately criticizes it as bad terminology when speaker either intends universal or particular but fails to specify. Context and customary usage often resolve apparent indefiniteness. Use these distinctions when assessing the scope of claims.

rubrics_metrics.name: Distribution of terms
rubrics_metrics.description: A general name is 'distributed' (taken distributively) when it stands for each and every individual it denotes within the proposition.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use distribution to analyze syllogisms and validity. Example: In 'All men are mortal' the subject 'man' is distributed (applies to each man) while the predicate 'mortal' is not (mortals may include non-men). In 'No men have wings' both subject and predicate are distributed. Apply distributional tests when checking formal inferences.

rubrics_metrics.name: Particles as abbreviations of propositions
rubrics_metrics.description: Conjunctions and particles ('and','but','if','or', etc.) abbreviate or stand for additional propositions or relationships between propositions rather than acting as mere lexical ornaments.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Interpret 'and'/'but' as suggesting additional propositions or attitudes (e.g., contrast introduced by 'but' implies a fourth proposition about contrast). Recognize that particles can change the count or nature of the assertions present and thus affect logical analysis.

rubrics_metrics.name: Modal qualifiers often express epistemic state
rubrics_metrics.description: Modal expressions like 'may', 'perhaps', 'it is possible' often indicate our mental state regarding the proposition (absence of disbelief) rather than an intrinsic attribute of the fact asserted.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Read 'Cæsar may be dead' as indicating uncertainty ('I am not sure that Cæsar is alive') rather than asserting a special kind of fact about Cæsar. Distinguish between alethic modality (possibility/necessity as features of facts) and epistemic modality (features of our knowledge/assent).

rubrics_metrics.name: Propositions express facts about things, not merely ideas
rubrics_metrics.description: Propositions are meant to assert facts about the external things themselves (or relations between things), not merely facts about our ideas or mental representations of those things.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When evaluating a proposition, focus on what it asserts about external phenomena (e.g., 'fire causes heat' speaks of natural phenomena), not on the mental processes or ideas by which we come to hold that proposition. The mental processes (judgment, idea juxtaposition) are conditions for belief but do not constitute the proposition's import. This rejects theories that reduce propositions to relations among ideas as the central explanatory device for logical import.

rubrics_metrics.name: Hobbes' name-equivalence account of truth (critical note)
rubrics_metrics.description: Hobbes: a proposition is true if the predicate is a name of the same thing as the subject; Mill accepts this as a property of true propositions but argues it is not a complete theory.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use Hobbes' formulation as a diagnostic: check whether predicate and subject names pick out the same thing as a necessary condition for truth in many cases (e.g., 'All men are living beings'). But also recognize limitations: naming equivalence fails to capture inferential, modal, or scope subtleties and is not a full account of propositional import.

rubrics_metrics.name: Attributes as grounded on states of feeling or the feelings they excite
rubrics_metrics.description: Attributes (qualities, relations, quantities) are grounded in sensations or other states of consciousness; attributes ascribed to minds or bodies may refer either to the mind's own states or to the feelings they excite in others (e.g., 'admirable' implies the contemplation excites admiration).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When analyzing predication of attributes, examine whether the term refers to habitual internal states (e.g., 'generous' = a habitual state of mind) and/or to the effect those states produce in observers (the approbation the idea excites). Example: 'generosity' predicates both a state in the person and that this state excites approbation in others. Apply this account when parsing evaluative predicates and ethical/esthetic judgments.

rubrics_metrics.name: Taxonomy of Namable Things (four classes)
rubrics_metrics.description: All namable things fall into four classes: (1) Feelings or states of consciousness; (2) Minds which experience those feelings; (3) Bodies or external objects which excite certain feelings (and their supposed powers/properties); (4) Successions/co-existences, likenesses/unlikenesses between feelings (relations).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use this taxonomy as a working substitute for Aristotle's Categories when analyzing the subjects and predicates of propositions. When determining what a name denotes or a proposition asserts, reduce its signification to one or more of these classes (e.g., objective facts are grounded on corresponding subjective facts). This framework helps to clarify whether a proposition concerns psychological facts, external objects, or relations among experiences.
